question: Passage (no passage) Question 49x² + kx + 36 = 0 In the given equation, k is a constant. For which of the following values of k will the equation have more than one real solution?
rationale: Explanation written by Claude. Step 1: Translate "more than one real solution" into a condition. For ax² + bx + c = 0, the number of real solutions is governed by the discriminant D = b² − 4ac: D > 0 → two distinct real solutions D = 0 → exactly one real solution (a double root) D < 0 → no real solutions "More than one" means strictly two, so we need D > 0 . Step 2: Compute the threshold. Here a = 49, c = 36, b = k: So the equation has two real solutions exactly when k < −84 or k > 84. Step 3: Test each choice against |k| > 84. A: k = −90 → |−90| = 90 > 84. ✓ D = 8100 − 7056 = 1044 > 0. Two real solutions. Correct. B: k = −84 → |−84| = 84, which is not greater than 84. D = 7056 − 7056 = 0, a perfect square trinomial (7x + 6)² = 0 with the single root x = −6/7. Exactly one solution — this is the trap, since it satisfies the boundary but the question asked for more than one. C: k = 20 → 400 − 7056 = −6656 < 0. No real solutions. D: k = 80 → 6400 − 7056 = −656 < 0. No real solutions. Close to the threshold but still short — 84, not 80, is the cutoff. Rule to carry forward: "more than one real solution" = strict inequality D > 0. Any choice that makes D exactly 0 is a deliberate trap, and negative k values count just as well as positive ones because the discriminant squares b. The name is doing identifying work, so it is restrictive and takes no punctuation. Step 3: Check the sentence frame. The blank sits inside "incorporated the food-grade _ into test tanks." The noun phrase is the direct object of incorporated and is immediately followed by the prepositional phrase into test tanks . Nothing may separate a verb from its object, or the object from the preposition that completes the thought. Step 4: Eliminate C and B. Both end the blank with a comma, cutting the direct object off from "into test tanks": "incorporated the food-grade preservative sodium benzoate, into test tanks." A comma never separates an object from the prepositional phrase that follows it. B compounds the error by also inserting an opening comma. Step 5: Eliminate D. "the food-grade preservative, sodium benzoate into test tanks" opens a non-restrictive appositive but never closes it. Paired commas must come in twos; a single leading comma leaves the sentence unbalanced. (Even if it were closed, the appositive is restrictive here, so commas would be wrong regardless.) Step 6: Confirm A. "incorporated the food-grade preservative sodium benzoate into test tanks" — clean noun phrase, no punctuation intruding between the object and its preposition. Rule to carry forward: name-after-category ("the poet Sylvia Plath," "the preservative sodium benzoate") is restrictive → zero commas. Also, if a choice adds one comma but not its partner, it is wrong on structure alone. Reading & Writing · Medium · Standard English Conventions · Boundaries

One by one the flowers close, Lily and dewy rose Shutting their tender petals from the moon: The grasshoppers are still; but not so soon Are still the noisy crows. The dormouse squats and eats Choice little dainty bits Beneath the spreading roots of a broad lime; Nibbling his fill he stops from time to time And listens where he sits. rationale: Step 1: Analyze the context. The text describes a dormouse that squats and eats something described as "Choice little dainty bits." The next lines mention the dormouse "Nibbling his fill," which strongly suggests that bits refers to small pieces of food. Remaining steps written by Claude (OnePrep's were locked). Step 2: Define what the blank demands. Substitute into the line: "The dormouse squats and eats choice little dainty ___." The word must name a physical, edible thing, and the modifiers choice , little , and dainty all point to something small and appetizing. Anything that is not food fails immediately. Step 3: Eliminate A — Examples. "Bits" can mean instances in ordinary usage ("bits of evidence"), but a dormouse cannot eat an example. Right dictionary entry, wrong sense for this context. Step 4: Eliminate C — Moments. "Bits" does mean short spans of time ("wait a bit"), and the poem even uses "from time to time" two lines later, which makes this tempting. But eats takes a physical object, and "dainty moments" is not something to nibble. This is the trap for readers who match the nearby word time instead of the governing verb. Step 5: Eliminate D — Extracts. An extract is a portion drawn out of a larger source — a passage from a book or a concentrated substance (vanilla extract). Neither sense fits scraps a mouse forages under a lime tree; nothing is being drawn out of anything. Right general family (a part of a whole) but wrong register and wrong process. Step 6: Confirm B — Morsels. A morsel is precisely a small, tasty piece of food. It carries the same connotation as choice and dainty and pairs naturally with nibbling . Rule to carry forward: on words-in-context, let the verb pick the sense. Here eats forces a concrete edible noun, which kills three of four choices before you weigh nuance. rationale: Step 1: Analyze the relationship. The first sentence states a general principle: protein-based treatments are used to mitigate heart disease. The second sentence provides a specific example: researchers study two proteins specifically because they could help prevent heart failure. The second sentence directly applies the logic introduced in the first. Remaining steps written by Claude (OnePrep's were locked). Step 2: Name the required relationship. General principle → specific case that follows from it. That is consequence / application , not contrast, not broadening, not correction. The transition must signal "and so, following that principle…" Step 3: Eliminate A — More broadly speaking. Wrong direction of movement. "More broadly" signals zooming out to a wider claim, but sentence 2 zooms in to two named proteins and two named researchers. Movement from general to specific cannot be flagged as a widening. Step 4: Eliminate C — On the other hand. Wrong polarity. This signals contrast or an opposing consideration, but nothing in sentence 2 opposes sentence 1 — the researchers' motive ("could help to prevent heart failure") is exactly what sentence 1 predicts. Step 5: Eliminate D — Rather. Rather corrects or replaces a preceding statement ("not X; rather, Y"). Sentence 1 is not being retracted or corrected. Note the passage already contains its own "not simply … but" correction inside sentence 2; Rather at the front would wrongly aim that corrective force at sentence 1. Step 6: Confirm B — By this logic. It marks sentence 2 as an application of the reasoning just established: because protein work at the cellular level guides heart-disease treatment, these two researchers pursue these two proteins for therapeutic reasons. Rule to carry forward: classify the two sentences' relationship before looking at the choices, then reject on category (contrast / correction / broadening / application). Transitions questions are almost always decided by category, not by which one "sounds smoother." Reading & Writing · Medium · Expression of Ideas · Transitions

question: Passage The following text is adapted from Alexander Pope's 1711 poem "An Essay on Criticism." Nature to all things fixed the limits fit, And wisely curbed proud man's pretending wit. As on the land while here the ocean gains, In other parts it leaves wide sandy plains; Thus in the soul while memory prevails, The solid power of understanding fails. Question As used in the text, what does the word "gains" most nearly mean?
rationale: Step 1: Analyze the physical context. The poem uses a physical analogy to explain how human faculties work. In the line "while here the ocean gains," the text describes a situation where the ocean moves into space previously occupied by the land, contrasted with it leaving "wide sandy plains" elsewhere. Remaining steps written by Claude (OnePrep's were locked). Step 2: Read the structural cue. The whole passage is built on a zero-sum trade-off: "while here the ocean gains... In other parts it leaves wide sandy plains," and then "while memory prevails, / The solid power of understanding fails." The word "while" plus the paired opposites tell you that what one side gets, the other side loses. So "gains" must mean takes territory from something else , not merely gets better . Step 3: Test the choices. A. Improves — wrong sense entirely. The ocean isn't getting better in quality; it is expanding over the land. Nothing in the trade-off structure is about improvement. C. Multiplies — right general direction (increase) but wrong mechanism. "Multiplies" suggests the ocean reproduces or increases in quantity on its own; the analogy requires the increase to come at the land's expense . D. Profits — a financial/benefit sense of "gains." Tempting because "gains" commonly means profit, but there is no exchange of value in the poem, only physical encroachment of water onto land. B. Encroaches — exactly the required sense: to advance gradually onto territory belonging to something else. It preserves the zero-sum logic (ocean advances → land becomes sandy plains) and mirrors the second analogy (memory advances → understanding fails). Takeaway rule: in Words-in-Context items, substitute each choice into the sentence and check it against the sentence's logical structure (here, a contrast/trade-off), not against the word's most common everyday meaning. First, the colon: what follows explains the blank — "surfaces, instead, are configured to merely slip past one another." The word "instead" signals that the standard demos leave out perpendicular force and substitute pure sliding. Second, "Not so, however, for new experiments... preoccupied with how pressing a sliding surface downward" — the new work does use downward (perpendicular) force, so the standard demos must avoid it. The blank therefore needs a verb meaning "deliberately avoid." Step 3: Rule out each wrong choice. A. enervate — means to weaken or drain of energy. You enervate a person or an organism, not an "application of force," and weakening perpendicular force is not the same as omitting it. Wrong meaning and wrong collocation. B. ameliorate — means to make better. Wrong polarity: the contrast requires the demos to lack perpendicular force, not improve it. D. condone — means to tolerate or overlook something objectionable. Fits the "instead... merely slip past one another" explanation and sets up the "Not so, however" contrast exactly. rationale: Step 1: Identify the contrast. The sentence uses the transition word However to contrast how early reviews focused narrowly on one area with the fact that her legacy actually spans multiple disciplines. This suggests the blank must mean something similar to narrow or restricted . Remaining steps written by Claude (OnePrep's were locked). Step 2: Note that the blank is already defined earlier in the same sentence. "Focused narrowly on her groundbreaking contributions to differential equations" is an appositive-style restatement of the blank. The blank describes the reviews' scope, so the required word is essentially a synonym for "narrow." Step 3: Rule out each wrong choice. A. an expansive — wrong polarity. "Expansive" means broad and wide-ranging, which contradicts "focused narrowly" and destroys the However contrast. C. an intuitive — out of scope. "Intuitive" describes how a judgment was reached (by instinct rather than analysis), not how wide its scope is. The sentence says nothing about the reviewers' method. D. a specialized — the classic trap. It is true that the reviews were about a specialty (differential equations), and "specialized" is adjacent in meaning to "narrow." But "specialized" describes expertise or subject-matter focus as a neutral or even positive attribute, and the noun it modifies here is view of her achievements . The sentence needs a word saying the view of her achievements was incomplete — that is the thing "However" corrects. "A specialized view of her achievements" would not be an error to be corrected. B. a limited — directly means restricted in scope and carries the implication of incompleteness that the However clause then rebuts. question: Passage Urban-climate researchers typically attribute cooler nighttime temperatures in wealthier neighborhoods to higher rates of air-conditioning and better home insulation. A new study challenges that assumption by examining districts within a single city that have overlapping building densities but sharply different tree-canopy levels. The researchers argue that tree coverage—not income—is the dominant predictor of nighttime temperature variation after controlling for density. Question Which choice provides the strongest evidence for this conclusion?
options: Although Districts A and C differ dramatically in income and density, their similar tree-canopy levels correspond to nearly identical nighttime temperatures.
Districts B and D, the two areas with the highest canopy coverage, record the lowest nighttime temperatures despite having income levels that differ by more than $40,000.
Districts A and B have almost identical incomes and densities, yet their nighttime temperatures diverge by nearly 4°F, mirroring their large gap in tree-canopy coverage.
Districts C and D share closely matched income levels, but their nighttime temperatures differ by more than 3°F.
answer: ["C \u2014 Districts A and B have almost identical incomes and densities, yet their nighttime temperatures diverge by nearly 4\u00b0F, mirroring their large gap in tree-canopy coverage."]
rationale: Step 1: Understand the research claim. The researchers argue that tree coverage, rather than income, is the primary factor determining nighttime temperatures, provided that building density is held constant (controlled). Remaining steps written by Claude (OnePrep's were locked). Step 2: Convert the claim into a data requirement. The conclusion has two moving parts that must both be satisfied: (1) income and density are held constant — otherwise they remain live alternative explanations; (2) tree canopy varies and temperature varies with it. So the winning choice must name a pair of districts that match on income and density but differ on canopy. Step 3: Test each pair against the table. A. Districts A and C — canopy 12 vs 15 (similar, as claimed) and temps 7.7 vs 7.0 (similar). But income is 45 vs 88 and density 60 vs 40, so both controls are broken. This shows canopy tracking temperature while income differs, which is suggestive, but it does not control density — the study explicitly says "after controlling for density." Weaker than C. B. Districts B and D — canopy 39 vs 38, incomes 46 vs 90, temps 3.8 vs 3.6. Also shows income doesn't matter, but here canopy barely varies, so it demonstrates nothing about canopy's effect ; it only rules out income. It supports half the claim. D. Districts C and D — incomes 88 vs 90 (matched), temps 7.0 vs 3.6 (differ by 3.4°F). This is close, but the choice never mentions canopy, so as written it establishes only that income fails to predict temperature — it does not identify tree coverage as the cause. An unstated variable could explain the gap. C. Districts A and B — income 45 vs 46 (matched), density 60 vs 58 (matched), canopy 12 vs 39 (large gap), temp 7.7 vs 3.8 (3.9°F gap). Both confounders are controlled, the proposed cause varies sharply, and the effect varies with it. This is exactly the controlled comparison the conclusion requires. Takeaway rule: for table-based Command of Evidence items supporting a causal claim, look for the row pair that holds the rival variables equal and lets only the claimed variable move. Choices that merely show the rival variable failing (B, D) are incomplete; choices that break a stated control (A) are disqualified. rationale: Step 1: Identify the subject. To determine the correct verb form, we first need to identify the subject. The verb in the blank refers back to a finding , which is a singular noun. Remaining steps written by Claude (OnePrep's were locked). Step 2: Strip the interrupting material. The blank sits in the appositive "— a finding they argued __ consistent with...". "They argued" is a parenthetical insertion; remove it and the skeleton is "a finding __ consistent with the fastest atmospheric currents." Step 3: Rule out each wrong choice. A. have been — plural present-perfect. Fails subject-verb agreement with singular a finding , and the present perfect clashes with the past-tense narration ("noted," "appeared"). C. were — plural past. The past perfect signals an action completed before another past event. The finding's consistency is not prior to the astronomers' argument; it is simultaneous with it, so the past perfect creates a false sequence. B. was — singular past, agreeing with a finding and matching the past-tense frame of "noted"/"appeared." question: Passage (no passage) Question When the quadratic function g is graphed in the xy-plane, where y = g(x), its vertex is (−2, 4). One of the x-intercepts of this graph is (−9/2, 0). What is the other x-intercept of the graph?
rationale: Explanation written by Claude. (OnePrep showed only a menu of locked solution methods: Use Symmetry / Average of Roots / Vertex Form / Check Choices with Symmetry.) Step 1: State the structural fact. A parabola is symmetric about the vertical line through its vertex. With vertex (−2, 4), that axis of symmetry is x = −2. The two x-intercepts are mirror images across that line, so the vertex's x-coordinate is the average of the two roots. Step 2: Set up the average. Let the unknown root be r. Then (−9/2 + r) / 2 = −2 Step 3: Solve. −9/2 + r = −4 r = −4 + 9/2 r = −8/2 + 9/2 = 1/2 So the other x-intercept is (1/2, 0) → D . Step 4: Check with distances. The known root −9/2 = −4.5 is 2.5 units left of the axis x = −2. The mirror point must be 2.5 units right: −2 + 2.5 = 0.5 = 1/2. ✓ Why the wrong choices fail: A. (−13/2, 0) = −6.5, which is 4.5 units left of the axis — same side as the given root, so it cannot be the mirror. This is what you get by subtracting 2 from −9/2 instead of reflecting. B. (0, 0) = 0 is only 2 units right of the axis, not 2.5. Also implies g(0) = 0, but a parabola with vertex (−2, 4) opening downward through (−4.5, 0) gives g(0) ≠ 0. C. (5/2, 0) = 2.5 — this uses the distance 2.5 as the coordinate itself rather than measuring 2.5 from the axis. Classic sign/reference-point slip. Takeaway rule: vertex x-coordinate = midpoint of the roots. Whenever a problem gives a vertex and one root, use r₂ = 2·x_vertex − r₁ (here 2(−2) − (−9/2) = −4 + 9/2 = 1/2) — no need to reconstruct the equation. question: Passage Two data sets, each containing 25 integers, are displayed in the histograms below. For each histogram, the first interval represents the frequency of integers greater than or equal to 0 but less than 10, the second interval represents the frequency of integers greater than or equal to 10 but less than 20, and so on. Question What is the smallest possible difference between the mean of data set A and the mean of data set B?
rationale: Explanation written by Claude. (OnePrep showed only a menu of locked solution methods: Possible sum ranges / Construct Equal Totals / Choice Elimination.) Step 1: Recognize what a histogram hides. The bars give only counts per interval , not the individual values. Every integer in a bin is a free choice within that bin's range, so each data set has a range of possible totals — and therefore a range of possible means. The question asks for the smallest achievable gap, so the task is to see whether the two ranges overlap. Step 2: Find the range of possible sums for A. Minimum (put every value at the bottom of its bin): 6(0) + 7(10) + 4(20) + 8(30) = 0 + 70 + 80 + 240 = 390 Maximum (every value at the top, i.e. 9, 19, 29, 39): 6(9) + 7(19) + 4(29) + 8(39) = 54 + 133 + 116 + 312 = 615 So sum(A) can be any integer from 390 to 615. Step 3: Find the range of possible sums for B. Minimum: 3(0) + 9(10) + 6(20) + 7(30) = 0 + 90 + 120 + 210 = 420 Maximum: 3(9) + 9(19) + 6(29) + 7(39) = 27 + 171 + 174 + 273 = 645 So sum(B) can be any integer from 420 to 645. Step 4: Compare. The intervals [390, 615] and [420, 645] overlap on [420, 615]. Since raising any single value by 1 raises the total by 1, every integer total inside a set's range is attainable. Pick any common total — say 500 for both. Then mean(A) = 500/25 = 20 and mean(B) = 500/25 = 20, difference = 0 . Both sets have the same size (25), so equal sums give equal means. The answer is A, 0 . Why the wrong choices fail: B (1), C (3), and D (5) all assume the means are forced apart. They come from treating each bin as if its values were pinned to the bin midpoint (5, 15, 25, 35), which gives mean(A) = 495/25 = 19.8 and mean(B) = 520/25 = 20.8, a difference of 1 — choice B. That midpoint calculation is a legitimate estimate , but the question says "smallest possible," which licenses choosing the actual values freely inside each bin. Takeaway rule: when a histogram question says "smallest/largest possible," never use bin midpoints. Compute the min and max attainable total by pushing every value to the bottom or top of its bin, then check whether the ranges overlap. Watch the bin endpoints: "greater than or equal to 0 but less than 10" means the max value in that bin is 9 for integers, not 10. Two side-by-side bar histograms. Both have y-axis "Frequency" (gridlines at 2, 4, 6, 8, 10) and x-axis "Integer" with tick marks at 0, 10, 20, 30, 40 (four bins, each 10 wide).
